prompt:
An atmospheric research capsule of mass 25.0 kg is dropped from rest from a stationary balloon at high altitude. The acceleration of free fall is 9.81 m s^-2.

(a) At time t = 4.00 s after release, telemetry records that the capsule has a downward speed of 28.0 m s^-1 and a downward acceleration of 3.80 m s^-2.
(i) Calculate the weight of the capsule. [1]
(ii) Calculate the upward drag force acting on the capsule at t = 4.00 s. [2]
(b) The capsule continues falling through the atmosphere until it reaches terminal velocity.
(i) State the magnitude of the acceleration and the magnitude of the drag force acting on the capsule at terminal velocity. [1]
(ii) On the same axes of a velocity-time graph, compare the curve for the capsule falling in air with the graph for an identical capsule dropped from rest in a vacuum. Identify two specific graphical differences. [2]

response_structure.description: Calculation of drag force at t = 4.00 s
Acceleration and drag force at terminal velocity
Comparison of velocity-time graphs in air vs vacuum

hints: Use W = mg with m = 25.0 kg and g = 9.81 m s^-2.
teacher_walkthrough: Step 2: Round to 3 significant figures: 245 N.
common_pitfalls: Using an approximate value of g = 10 m s^-2 instead of Cambridge standard 9.81 m s^-2.

hints: Find the net downward force using F_net = ma.
Relate net force to weight and drag: F_net = W - D.
teacher_walkthrough: Step 1: Calculate net force: F_net = ma = 25.0 x 3.80 = 95.0 N.
Step 2: Relate forces: F_net = W - D => D = W - F_net.
common_pitfalls: Equating drag directly to ma without accounting for weight.

hints: Recall that at terminal velocity forces are balanced.
teacher_walkthrough: Step 2: Drag force equals weight = 245 N.
common_pitfalls: Writing acceleration as 9.81 m s^-2 at terminal velocity.

hints: Think about the gradient of both graphs and how speed changes at large times.
teacher_walkthrough: Step 1: Note that in vacuum, v-t graph is a straight line through origin with constant gradient g.
Step 2: In air, initial gradient is g, but gradient decreases continuously.
Step 3: In vacuum, velocity increases indefinitely without limit; in air, velocity approaches a horizontal asymptote (terminal velocity).
common_pitfalls: Drawing the curve in air starting with zero slope instead of slope g.

hints: Compare graph shapes: straight line vs decreasing gradient curve leveling off.
solution:
(a)(i) Weight W = mg = 25.0 kg x 9.81 m s^-2 = 245 N.
(a)(ii) F_net = ma = 25.0 kg x 3.80 m s^-2 = 95.0 N.
F_net = W - D => D = W - F_net = 245.25 N - 95.0 N = 150 N.
(b)(i) Acceleration = 0 m s^-2; Drag force = 245 N.
(b)(ii) 1. In a vacuum, the graph is a straight line with a constant gradient of 9.81 m s^-2, whereas in air the gradient decreases continuously from 9.81 m s^-2.
2. In a vacuum, velocity increases indefinitely without limit, whereas in air the curve approaches a horizontal plateau/asymptote at terminal velocity.
teacher_walkthrough: Step 4: (b)(ii) Vacuum is straight line (constant slope g), air is curve with decreasing slope leveling off to horizontal asymptote.

mark_scheme.criterion: Acceleration = 0 m s^-2 and drag force = 245 N (or equals weight)
Vacuum graph is a straight line of constant gradient (9.81 m s^-2), whereas air graph has continuously decreasing gradient
Vacuum velocity increases without limit, whereas air curve reaches / approaches a constant horizontal asymptote (terminal velocity)
